P.S.—Do let me know about the bows. Jennings maintains that they are fashionable.

Lord Arthur wore such a grave and miserable expression over the letter that the Duchess burst into laughter.

'My dear Arthur,' she exclaimed, 'I shall never let you see another young lady's letter! But what am I to say of the clock? I consider it an excellent invention, and should quite like one of my own.'

'I have no great opinion of them,' Lord Arthur answered with a melancholy smile; then, kissing his mother, he went out.

Upstairs he threw himself upon a sofa, and tears gathered in his eyes. He had exerted himself to the utmost to commit this murder, yet both attempts had failed, through no fault of his. He had endeavoured to fulfil his duty, but Destiny herself seemed to have betrayed him. The fruitlessness of good intentions, the uselessness of aspiring to nobility, weighed heavily upon him. Perhaps the wisest course would be to abandon the marriage entirely. Sybil would be hurt, certainly, but pain could not truly spoil a character as noble as hers. For himself, what did it signify? There was always a war in which a man might perish, a cause for which he might sacrifice his life; and since life offered him no delight, death inspired no fear. Destiny could accomplish his doom herself. He would lift no finger to assist her.

At half past seven he dressed and made his way to the club. Surbiton was there among a company of young men, and he was compelled to dine with them. Their inconsequential talk and frivolous jokes held no interest for him. As soon as coffee appeared, he invented an appointment and escaped. On his way out, the hall porter gave him a letter from Herr Winckelkopf, inviting him to visit the following evening and inspect an explosive umbrella that detonated the instant it opened. This newest invention had only just arrived from Geneva. He ripped the letter into little pieces. He had resolved to attempt no further experiments. Afterward he wandered towards the Thames Embankment, where he sat beside the river for hours. Through a mane of tawny cloud the moon gazed like the eye of a lion; countless stars glittered across the hollow sky like powdered gold scattered over a purple dome. Occasionally a barge swung into the muddy current and drifted off with the tide, while the railway signals shifted from green to scarlet as trains sped shrieking over the bridge.

Body and soul, soul and body—what mysteries they presented! The soul contained something animal, while the body knew moments of spirituality. Sensation could ennoble, and thought could debase. Who could determine where an impulse of the flesh ended and one of the spirit began? How superficial were the arbitrary distinctions made by commonplace psychologists! Yet how hard it was to choose among the assertions of their different schools! Was the soul a shadow inhabiting the dwelling of sin? Or did the body exist within the soul, as Giordano Bruno believed? Spirit's division from matter was mysterious, and its conjunction with matter no less so.

He wondered whether psychology might ever become a science so exact that every small mechanism of life lay open to our inspection. At present, we invariably misunderstood ourselves and seldom comprehended anyone else. Experience possessed no moral worth. It was simply the title people bestowed upon their errors. Moralists generally treated it as a warning, attributed to it some ethical influence upon the shaping of character, and commended it for teaching us what to pursue and what to shun. Yet experience had no force to propel us. It was no more an active agent than conscience. All it actually proved was that the future would repeat the past, and the sin we had committed once with disgust would be repeated often with pleasure.

To him it was evident that experiment alone could lead to a scientific examination of the passions. Certainly Dorian Gray offered a subject ideally suited to his purposes, one that promised abundant and rewarding discoveries. His abrupt, extravagant love for Sibyl Vane was a psychological occurrence of considerable interest. Curiosity unquestionably played a large part—curiosity and a craving for unfamiliar experiences—but the passion was far from simple; it was exceedingly complex. Whatever belonged in it to the purely sensual instincts of youth had been altered by imagination, converted into something that appeared to the boy himself entirely removed from the senses, and was therefore all the more perilous. The passions whose beginnings we concealed from ourselves exercised the greatest tyranny over us. Our feeblest motives were those whose true character we recognized. Often, when we imagined ourselves to be experimenting upon other people, we were in reality experimenting upon ourselves.

As Lord Henry sat absorbed in these reflections, someone knocked, and his valet came in to remind him that the hour had arrived to dress for dinner.

"Certainly not," Duff answered.

"And if I translate 'yokel' for the ladies, I take it you mean that this attempt wasn't made by someone from the country?" Mr. Losberne asked with a smile.

"That's right, sir," said Blathers. "Is that everything about the robbery?"

"Everything," the doctor replied.

"Now, what's this about a boy the servants keep mentioning?" Blathers asked.

"Nothing whatsoever," said the doctor. "One of the frightened servants got it into his head that the boy had something to do with the attempted break-in. But it's nonsense—complete absurdity."

"Easily settled, if that's so," Duff observed.

"He's perfectly right," Blathers said, nodding in agreement and idly clicking the handcuffs together like castanets. "Who is this boy? What does he say about himself? Where did he come from? He didn't fall out of the sky, did he, sir?"

"Of course not," the doctor replied, glancing nervously at the two ladies. "I know his entire history, but we can discuss that shortly. First, I imagine you'd like to see where the thieves tried to enter?"

"Certainly," said Mr. Blathers. "We'd better inspect the property before questioning the servants. That's our usual procedure."

Lights were brought, and Blathers and Duff, accompanied by the local constable, Brittles, Giles, and, in short, everyone else, entered the small room at the end of the passage and looked out through the window. Next they went around across the lawn and looked in through it. Then they requested a candle to examine the shutter, followed by a lantern to follow the footprints, followed by a pitchfork to probe the bushes. Having completed these operations before their breathlessly attentive audience, they returned inside. Mr. Giles and Brittles were then made to stage a dramatic reenactment of their parts in the previous night's events. They performed it some six times, contradicting each other on no more than one significant detail the first time and no more than a dozen the last. Once this achievement was complete, Blathers and Duff emptied the room and held a lengthy conference. In secrecy and solemnity, their discussion made a consultation of eminent doctors on the most difficult problem in medicine look like child's play.

Meanwhile, the doctor paced the adjoining room in a state of considerable anxiety, while Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched him with worried faces.

"Honestly," he said, stopping after a great many rapid turns, "I scarcely know what to do."
